newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: PRESS DIGEST - Czech Republic - March 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Czech Republic - March 27.

text.p: HOSPODARSKE NOVINY - The government yesterday discussed three fundamental norms that are to form the backbone of national security. The government passed a national defence strategy; a constitutional law to address national security and voted on a concept of land and air defence. The cabinet instructed Defence Minister Miloslav Vyborny to develop a timetable and budget list before implementing the changes.

- Parliament yesterday rejected a proposal by the Social Democrats to lower the retirement age to pre-1996 levels. According to the current programme, in place until the year 2007, men will be able to retire at the age of 62, while women will be allowed to retire between the ages of 57-61, depending upon the number of children they have.

- The IFC announced that it will reduce its presence in the Czech Republic and focus more on states with less developed economies such as the Ukraine and Albania. The IFC says that it will contiune to cooperate with leasing companies and other non-banking firms that have problems obtaining capital.

MLADA FRONTA DNES - Mortgages for homes will continue to be an unaffordable luxury for most Czech families. Families seeking to buy a home would have to settle for living on, or near the poverty line as most of their earnings would be diverted to paying off their mortgage.
- The finance ministry suspects the management of the Moravskocesky investment fund of fraud. The ministry suspects that the fund has been illegally manipulating assets of depositors.

- The government announced that it will buy new supersonic fighters for the Czech airforce which would be the largest single defence purchase in the country's history. Premier Klaus said that he would like to see the aircraft enter full service by the year 2003.

PRAVO - Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy said yesterday that the Czech Republic will not be intimidated by comments made by Russian state gas company, Gazprom. Earlier in the week Gazprom's CEO, Juri Komarov threatened that the Russians would raise gas prices to match those of Norway if the Czechs begin taking supplies of Norwegian gas. Dlouhy said that at current rates being offered by the Norwegians, the Russians would have to adapt by lowering their current price for gas.
